title: Of one defect in our government
paragraphs: My late father, a man whose only advantages were experience and his own natural gifts, but who had a very clear judgment, once told me he had had thoughts of trying to introduce this practice: that in every city there should be a fixed place where anyone in need of anything could go and have their business registered by an officer appointed for the purpose. For example: I need a buyer for my pearls; I need someone with pearls to sell; this one wants company on the road to Paris; that one is looking for a servant of such-and-such a kind; another for a master; another for some particular craftsman. Some looking for one thing, some for another, each according to his need. Without doubt, these mutual notices would be of no small benefit to public exchange and communication. There are always parties searching for one another, and for want of knowing each other's needs they are left in real distress.

I have heard — to the great shame of the age we live in — that two of the most learned men of our day died so poor they had hardly bread to put in their mouths: Lilius Gregorius Giraldus in Italy and Sebastianus Castalio in Germany. I am sure there are a thousand men who would have invited them into their families on advantageous terms, or relieved them where they were, had they only known of their want. The world is not so universally corrupted; I know a man who would gladly use the estate his ancestors left him, for as long as fortune allows him to enjoy it, to shelter rare and remarkable people of any kind whom misfortune sometimes persecutes to the last extreme, from the dangers of want — at least to place them in such a condition that they would have to be hard to please not to be content.

My father had this rule in his domestic affairs (which I know how to praise but by no means how to imitate): besides the day-book or household memorandum, where the small accounts, payments, and expenses that don't require a secretary's hand were entered, and which the steward kept, he had whoever wrote for him keep a journal, setting down in it all the noteworthy events and daily memorials of the history of the house. Very pleasant to look over when time begins to wear things out of memory, and very useful sometimes to settle a doubt about when this or that began, or ended; what visitors came, and when they left; our journeys, absences, marriages, deaths; news good or bad received; changes among the principal servants, and so on. An old custom, which I think it would do everyone good to revive in his own house. I see I was very foolish to neglect it.
